The megrim, Lepidorhombus whiffiagonis, is a commercially valuable flatfish distributed across the northeastern Atlantic, and its life-history parameters have been characterized through extensive field sampling and otolith-based ageing studies. Females deposit pelagic eggs following a spawning event, and the fertilised ova measure approximately 1 millimetre in diameter. Based on this egg size, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0005236 grams [Wwb = 0.0005236 grams], representing the mass of the yolk-dependent embryo immediately after chorion rupture. The larval period begins with the yolk-sac larva emerging and initiating a lecithotrophic phase, during which the duration from hatching to the onset of exogenous feeding has been documented at 7 days [ab = 7 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This brief endotrophic interval reflects the relatively small yolk reserves typical of species that produce numerous small eggs, a strategy that prioritises fecundity over per-offspring investment.

Growth trajectories derived from length-at-age data indicate that megrim achieve a maximum recorded total length of 60 centimetres [Li = 60 centimetres] in wild populations, with the largest individuals typically representing older, slow-growing females. The length-weight relationship fitted to regional survey data follows the form W = 0.00468 * L^3.09, from which a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 1461 grams [Wwi = 1461 grams] is estimated for the largest specimens. This asymptotic body mass is comparable to values reported for other commercially fished pleuronectiforms of similar maximum size in the North Sea and Celtic Sea. Somatic growth is most rapid during the first few years of life, after which the growth rate decelerates markedly as individuals approach their final dimensions, a pattern commonly observed in iteroparous teleosts that allocate increasing resources toward reproductive output as they mature.

Puberty in megrim is defined by the onset of gametogenesis, with histological examination of gonadal tissue revealing that males and females first exhibit vitellogenesis and spermiation at a total length of 25.8 centimetres [Lp = 25.8 centimetres]. Applying the species-specific length-weight relationship, the wet weight at puberty for an individual of this length is calculated as 108 grams [Wwp = 108 grams], indicating that fish must reach a critical mass before reproductive activation occurs. The transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively viable organism is a gradual process, with some individuals showing signs of gonadal recrudescence slightly earlier or later depending on local environmental conditions and food availability. This pubertal size threshold aligns well with values reported for other Lepidorhombus species and suggests a life-history strategy in which the onset of reproduction is contingent on achieving a minimum body size sufficient to support the energetic demands of spawning.

Reproductive output in megrim has been quantified through analysis of fecundity and spawning frequency, revealing that mature females produce an average of 640,000 eggs per spawning batch [N_R_i = 640,000 eggs per spawning batch] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. They undergo approximately 365 spawning events each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events each year], a reproductive schedule that reflects a daily spawning pattern. Spawning adults migrate toward deeper continental shelf waters during the winter months, and the pelagic eggs and planktonic larvae drift with prevailing currents before metamorphosis triggers the pelagic-benthic transition, after which the post-settlement juveniles take up residence on sandy or muddy substrates. The iteroparous nature of this species, combined with its substantial batch fecundity, suggests a capacity for population resilience under moderate fishing pressure, though recruitment variability remains high due to the dependence of early life stages on oceanographic conditions.

Longevity estimates for megrim, derived from otolith annuli counts of the oldest individuals sampled in scientific trawl surveys, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] for fish inhabiting waters at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, combined with delayed maturity and high fecundity, classifies the species as having a moderately slow life-history pace among flatfishes. Senescent changes in older individuals include reduced reproductive output and increased incidence of parasitic infections, though the exact timing of reproductive senescence is poorly documented. Comparative data from related pleuronectiforms suggest that the maximum age recorded here is at the upper end of what might be expected for a species of this body size, possibly reflecting the relatively cold, stable thermal environment of its preferred depth range, which may slow metabolic processes and contribute to extended longevity.
